units.translation: After adverbs and particles with another word
After verbs with another word connected
δέ [but] placed fourth
Hermann restored it placed fifth
δέ [but] combined with other particles
δ᾽ αὖ [but again] answering to preceding μέν [on the one hand]
δέ γε [but at least] and δὲ – γε [but – at least]
δὲ δή [but indeed]
δ᾽ οὖν [but then]
καὶ δέ [and also]
where σχολή γάρ [for leisure] could have been said, but σχολή δέ [but leisure] is no less apt. Hermann discussed this usage in his notes on Viger, p. 675.

Since, however, the supply of examples of this kind is infinite in any writers you please, and to enumerate them all in lexicons would be a useless diligence, we shall produce examples from the hundred Aeschylean instances in the single play Prometheus, of which no fewer similar ones will be found in the remaining plays by anyone who wishes to examine them. Thus, then,
(where οὐ κατ᾿ ἰσχύν [not by force] and δόλῳ δέ [but by cunning], i.e. ἀλλὰ δόλῳ [but by cunning], are opposed to each other)
where δέ [but] five times in succession
where after what Orestes had said the chorus continues
where the chorus answers Danaus

for ἐμὴ δὲ μήτηρ [but my mother] the sense requires ἐμή γε μήτηρ [my mother at least], which Porson restored, just as at line 841 Portus correctly wrote μόρον γ᾽ Ορέστου [the fate of Orestes] for μόρον δ᾽ [but the fate].

Elmsley discussed accurately this use of the particle δέ [but], which in places of this kind copyists sometimes changed to τε [and], in his note on Euripides, Medea 940, p. 225: πατρὸς νέαν γυναῖκα, δεσπότιν τ᾿ ἐμήν [my father's new wife, and my mistress], where since γυναῖκα [wife] and δεσπότιν [mistress] are said of the same person, δέ [but] was necessary, which Elmsley restored. But correctly at line 17 is read προδοὺς γὰρ αὑτοῦ τέκνα δεσπότιν τ᾽ ἐμήν [for having betrayed his own children and my mistress], since Jason's children are different from his wife.
After ἐπεί [when]

where Porson rightly deleted δέ [but] after κρατηθείς [having been conquered], nor does the scholiast seem to have read it. There is a different error at Agamemnon 12, where after a sentence beginning with εὔτ᾽ ἂν δὲ [but whenever] the verb λύζω [I sob] placed in the apodosis has fallen out, about which will be discussed under that word.
After ὡς [as]

where with a change of construction the preceding words ἀρωγή – παρῆν [help – was present] are continued by the final words αὐτοὶ δὲ παίοντο [but they themselves were struck], the apodosis of ὡς δὲ ἤθροιστο [but when they had gathered] being omitted.

Nor can μέν [on the one hand] be said to be omitted where either opposites are set against each other by δέ [but] alone, or the same or similar word is placed in each part of the sentence, although in such places μὲν – δέ [on the one hand – but on the other] is very frequent, as the examples cited under the word μέν show.
Thus after the article and a substantive or adjective
i.e. σοὶ δὲ, Ηφαιστε [but to you, Hephaestus]. Thus Sophocles more often, about which I have spoken in my Lexicon Sophocleum p. 109, following Porson on Euripides, Orestes 614.
After a vocative and an imperative
After a noun with the participle ὤν [being]
After two substantives in different cases
After two adjectives
and so with the remaining prepositions
where Porson rightly [read] ὥστ᾽ [so that].
Thus Wellauer rightly for δ᾽ ἄν [but would].
where in M is read δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν λειβομένα [but from her slender eyes shedding tears], which does not fit the meter.
